question: How do LLMs work?
reference: An LLM is a Transformer network trained to predict the next token on huge text corpora (self-supervised pre-training). Text is split into tokens, each token becomes a vector, and attention layers relate each position to the previous ones to produce a probability distribution over the next token. Generation is autoregressive: sample a token, append it to the context, repeat. After pre-training, post-training (instruction tuning, RLHF/DPO) makes the model useful and safe in conversation. The model has no memory beyond its context window and only 'knows' what its weights have compressed, hence hallucinations and the need for RAG or tools.
key_points: Tokenization then embeddings; Transformer architecture with attention
Pre-training objective: predict the next token on a massive corpus
Autoregressive generation, token by token, with sampling
Post-training (instruction tuning, RLHF/DPO) to follow instructions
Limits: no memory outside the context, frozen knowledge, hallucinations
common_mistakes: Describing the LLM as a database that 'looks up' answers
Forgetting the pre-training / post-training distinction
Saying the model learns during the conversation

question: What is temperature and top-p sampling? How do they affect outputs?
reference: At each step the model produces logits over the vocabulary. Temperature divides the logits before the softmax: T < 1 sharpens the likely tokens (more deterministic, repetitive outputs), T > 1 flattens the distribution (more diversity, more errors), T = 0 amounts to greedy decoding. Top-p (nucleus sampling) keeps only the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, then samples within it: it cuts the long tail of unlikely tokens. Tune one or the other depending on the task: extraction/code -> low temperature; brainstorming -> higher. Even at T = 0 the output is not guaranteed identical (floating-point computation, batching).
key_points: Temperature: scales the logits before the softmax; low = deterministic, high = diversity
Top-p: samples within the smallest token set of cumulative probability p (cuts the tail)
Choice depends on the task: low for extraction/code/classification, higher for creativity
Determinism is not guaranteed even at temperature 0
common_mistakes: Confusing top-p and top-k
Believing temperature 0 guarantees an identical output
Saying temperature changes the model's knowledge

question: What is the context window and what happens when you exceed it? How do you handle long documents?
reference: The context window is the maximum number of tokens (prompt + answer) the model can process in one request. Beyond it, the API returns an error or the client truncates, often losing the beginning; and even under the limit, quality degrades on very long contexts ('lost in the middle'), with cost and latency growing with size. For a long document: split into chunks (by structure, with overlap), load only the relevant passages (RAG), summarize hierarchically (map-reduce), or make several targeted passes; count tokens before the call and keep room for the answer.
key_points: Definition: limit on input + output tokens per request
Overflow: error or truncation, information loss; degradation and cost even before the limit
Strategies: chunking, RAG (load only what is relevant), hierarchical summary / map-reduce
Count tokens and reserve room for the output
common_mistakes: Thinking a large-window model lets you paste everything in
Forgetting that the output counts towards the window

question: How do you do memory management and context management with LLMs?
reference: The model is stateless: all 'memory' has to be re-injected into the prompt. Distinguish working memory (the conversation history, truncated or summarized as it grows: sliding window, progressive summary, compaction), long-term memory (facts about the user or the project stored outside the model, retrieved by vector search or by keys, and injected selectively) and retrieval tools (RAG). Good practice: keep the system prompt and stable information at the beginning (cache), put the most useful information near the question, clean up large tool results, and evaluate what the memory actually brings.
key_points: The LLM is stateless: all context must be re-injected on every call
Working memory: truncated / summarized / compacted history
External long-term memory (database, vectors) injected selectively
Token budget management: prioritize, clean up, place the important part near the question
Prompt caching: stable part first
common_mistakes: Believing the model remembers previous conversations by itself
Putting everything into the context without selection or summary

question: What's RAG? Explain the complete process.
reference: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) makes the LLM answer from documents retrieved at query time rather than from its weights alone. Ingestion: collect the documents, clean them, split them into chunks, compute an embedding per chunk and index it (vector database, often complemented by a BM25 lexical index). Query: embed the question, retrieve the k closest chunks (hybrid + optional reranking), build a prompt with the question and the passages, generate an answer that cites its sources. Benefits: up-to-date and private knowledge, traceability, fewer hallucinations. Watch points: quality of chunking, retrieval and context window, and separate evaluation of the two stages.
key_points: Ingestion: cleaning, chunking, embeddings, indexing
Query: embed the question, retrieve the k relevant passages (hybrid, reranking)
Generation: prompt = question + passages, grounded answer with citations
Why: private / fresh data, traceability, fewer hallucinations
Evaluate retrieval and generation separately
common_mistakes: Describing RAG as fine-tuning
Forgetting the ingestion / chunking stage
Not mentioning evaluation or failure points

question: Text vs Vector search. When would you use each?
reference: Text search (BM25, inverted index) relies on exact terms: excellent for identifiers, codes, proper nouns, jargon, short precise queries; transparent, fast, no model needed. Vector search compares embeddings: it captures meaning (synonyms, paraphrases, natural-language questions, multilingual) but misses rare exact matches and depends on the embedding model. In practice you combine both (hybrid search, RRF fusion) then rerank with a cross-encoder. Choose according to the nature of queries and documents, and measure on an evaluation set.
key_points: Text/BM25: exact terms, identifiers, names, jargon; fast and explainable
Vector: semantic similarity, paraphrases, multilingual; depends on the embedding model
Complementary weaknesses: vocabulary vs exact match
Hybrid + reranking as a sensible default, validated by evaluation
common_mistakes: Presenting vector search as always superior
Ignoring the need for exact matches (references, numbers)

question: You're making a system for huge PDF reports. How would you process them?
reference: First extract cleanly: a PDF parser with layout detection (headings, columns, tables, figures), OCR for scans, tables extracted as structure (CSV/markdown) rather than flat text. Keep metadata (title, section, page, date) for filtering and citations. Split by structure (sections, paragraphs) with controlled size and overlap, keeping the hierarchical context (section title inside the chunk). Index hybrid, possibly with a summary per section for two-level search. Process in an asynchronous, idempotent pipeline (large volumes), deduplicate, and evaluate extraction on a sample because that is where most information gets lost.
key_points: Robust extraction: layout, tables, OCR when scanned
Metadata (page, section) kept for filtering and citing
Structured chunking with overlap and hierarchical context
Asynchronous, idempotent, deduplicated ingestion pipeline
Evaluate extraction and retrieval quality on a sample
common_mistakes: Splitting into fixed-size chunks regardless of structure
Forgetting tables and scanned documents

question: How would you handle the problem of a model hallucinating when no information is found in the given context?
reference: Several layers: explicitly instruct the model to answer only from the provided passages and to say 'I don't know' otherwise, with a mandatory citation format; filter upstream with a relevance threshold (if no passage passes it, answer that nothing was found or ask a clarifying question); verify grounding downstream (an LLM judge or an NLI model checks that each claim is supported by a passage); improve retrieval (hybrid, reranking, query rewriting) to reduce no-context cases; measure the rate of ungrounded answers on an evaluation set that includes unanswerable questions.
key_points: Explicit instruction: rely on the context, admit missing information
Retrieval relevance threshold / 'nothing found' detection
Downstream grounding check (judge, NLI, mandatory citations)
Improve retrieval to reduce empty cases
Evaluation set including unanswerable questions
common_mistakes: Just adding 'do not hallucinate' to the prompt
Not testing questions whose answer is not in the corpus

question: What are common RAG failure points and how do you debug them?
reference: Failures sort by stage. Ingestion: broken extraction, chunks that cut an idea, missing metadata, stale index. Retrieval: the right information exists but is not retrieved (bad embedding, poorly phrased query, k too small, filter too strict) or is drowned by irrelevant passages. Generation: the passage is there but the model ignores it, mixes it up or extrapolates; context too long; answer format. Debugging = instrumenting each stage: trace the query, the retrieved chunks and their scores, the final prompt; build a question set with expected passages to measure retrieval recall separately from answer quality; look at failure cases one by one before optimizing.
key_points: Ingestion/chunking failures (splitting, extraction, stale index)
Retrieval failures: right passage missing or poorly ranked
Generation failures: context ignored, mixed up, extrapolated
Observability: trace chunks, scores and final prompt
Evaluate retrieval (recall@k) and generation separately, analyze failures
common_mistakes: Switching the generation model when the problem is in retrieval
Optimizing without an evaluation set or traces

question: How do you handle citations and source attribution in a RAG system?
reference: Give each passage a stable identifier (document, section, page, URL) and pass it in the prompt with its content; ask the model for a structured answer where each claim references the identifiers used (JSON format or [1] markers); downstream, check that the cited identifiers exist and that the cited text supports the claim (overlap comparison or NLI judge), drop invalid citations; show the source excerpts to the user so they can verify. Some APIs offer native passage-level citations. Measuring citation precision is part of the evaluation.
key_points: Stable identifiers per chunk passed in the prompt
Structured answer: claims linked to identifiers
Downstream check: citation exists and supports the claim
Excerpts shown to the user; citation precision metrics
common_mistakes: Trusting generated citations without checking them
Citing the whole document instead of the passage

question: What is semantic caching?
reference: A classic cache only helps when the query is identical; a semantic cache stores (query embedding, answer) pairs and returns the cached answer when a new query is close enough (cosine similarity above a threshold). It reduces cost and latency on frequent, rephrased questions. Risks: serving an answer to a close but different question (the threshold is tuned on an evaluation set, and entities matter: 'price of plan A' != 'price of plan B'), stale answers (TTL, invalidation when documents change), personalization (do not share context-dependent answers between users). Distinct from the API's prompt caching, which caches the token prefix.
key_points: Cache keyed by embedding; hit when similarity > threshold
Gain: cost and latency on recurring rephrased queries
Risks: semantic false positives (entities, negations), freshness, personalization
Threshold tuning and invalidation; different from prompt caching
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the API's prompt caching
Ignoring false positives when an entity changes

question: How do you scale a RAG system to 10M+ articles?
reference: Ingestion: distributed, incremental pipeline (message queues, embedding batches, idempotency, version tracking). Index: distributed vector database with an approximate index (HNSW, IVF-PQ) and quantization to fit in memory; partition by tenant, language or date; combine with metadata filters and a lexical index. Query: two-stage search (fast candidates then reranking on a few dozen), cache of frequent queries, limits on k and on context size. Freshness: incremental updates, deletion of obsolete documents. Observability and cost: measure p95 latency, recall on an evaluation set, cost per query; size embeddings and storage.
key_points: Distributed, incremental, idempotent ingestion
ANN index (HNSW/IVF-PQ), quantization, partitioning, metadata filters
Two-stage search: fast candidates then reranking
Freshness and deletion of obsolete documents
Measure: p95 latency, recall, cost per query
common_mistakes: Proposing exact (brute-force) search over 10M vectors
Forgetting incremental index updates

question: What are the key tradeoffs when designing a RAG system?
reference: Chunk size: small = precise retrieval but fragmented context; large = more context but noise and cost. Number of passages k and context size: recall vs cost, latency and dilution. Retrieval quality vs cost: simple BM25 vs embeddings vs hybrid + reranker. Freshness vs indexing cost. Generation model: large, accurate and expensive vs small and fast. Precision vs coverage: a strict relevance threshold reduces hallucinations but increases 'I don't know' answers. Simplicity vs sophistication (agentic RAG, multiple queries) to be justified by measurements. The right setting depends on the use case and is decided with an evaluation set.
key_points: Chunk size and overlap: precision vs context
k and context length: recall vs cost/latency/dilution
Retrieval method: simplicity/cost vs quality (hybrid, reranking)
Generation model: quality vs cost/latency
Relevance threshold: hallucinations vs abstentions; arbitrate everything by evaluation
common_mistakes: Presenting one configuration as universal
Not mentioning cost and latency

question: What makes an AI system agentic?
reference: A system is agentic when the LLM itself decides the steps to reach a goal: it observes a state, chooses an action (call a tool, search, write), observes the result and iterates until a stop condition. The loop is driven by the model, not by a sequence of calls coded in advance (workflow). Ingredients: goal, tool-calling ability, observe-act loop, memory/state, stop criteria. It is a continuum, from a fixed workflow to an autonomous agent; more autonomy = more flexibility but less predictability, more cost and more risk, hence guardrails.
key_points: The model dynamically chooses actions (observe -> act -> observe loop) instead of a coded flow
Tool calls to act on the environment
State/memory and stop condition
Workflow -> agent continuum; autonomy against predictability, cost, risk
common_mistakes: Calling any LLM call with a tool an 'agent'
Forgetting the loop and the stop condition

question: What are the essential components of an agent beyond an LLM?
reference: Tools with clear descriptions and schemas (plus their execution, argument validation, error handling); an orchestration loop (turn management, parallel calls, stops); memory and context management (history, summary, long-term memory, retrieval); persistent state and resume points; guardrails (permissions, sandbox, cost and iteration limits, human validation for sensitive actions); observability (traces of each turn, costs, latency); and evaluation (task sets, success metrics). Often also a planner or sub-agents.
key_points: Well-described tools + safe, validated execution
Orchestration loop with stop conditions
Memory and context management, persistent state
Guardrails: permissions, sandbox, budgets, human in the loop
Observability and evaluation
common_mistakes: Listing only 'prompt + tools'
Forgetting observability and cost limits

question: How do agents decide which tool to use?
reference: The model receives the tool definitions (name, description, argument schema) in its request and, from the goal and the context, generates a structured call (tool_use) with the arguments; the choice therefore relies on the quality of the descriptions, examples and system prompt. Good practice: precise descriptions stating when (not) to use the tool, unambiguous names, few overlapping tools, strict schemas validated client-side, informative tool results (including errors) so the model can correct itself. With many tools: grouping, deferred loading or tool search. And evaluate the rate of correct tool choice on test cases.
key_points: Tool definitions in the prompt -> structured call generated by the model
Quality of descriptions and names, non-overlapping, with use cases
Argument validation and actionable error returns
Handling many tools: grouping, deferred loading
Measure tool-selection quality
common_mistakes: Believing the model 'executes' the tool itself
Neglecting the impact of descriptions on selection

question: When agent is the wrong solution?
reference: When the task is well specified and repeatable (a fixed workflow or a single LLM call is enough, cheaper and predictable); when the cost of an error is high without control or rollback; when latency or budget are constrained (an agent multiplies calls); when there is no good way to verify the result (tests, review); when the model is not reliable on this kind of task; or when a deterministic solution exists (rules, SQL). Rule: start with the simplest option, add autonomy only once value and viability are demonstrated.
key_points: Task specifiable in advance -> workflow or single call
High error cost without control/rollback
Latency and cost constraints
No way to verify the result; existing deterministic solution
Start simple, escalate only when needed
common_mistakes: Seeing only the benefits of autonomy
Ignoring the cost multiplied by the number of iterations

question: How do you explain agentic systems to non-technical stakeholders?
reference: By analogy: an assistant given a goal, who has a set of tools (query a database, send an email) and rules (what it may do alone, what needs approval), and who works step by step while checking its results. Stress what it can and cannot do, the guardrails, the fact that it can be wrong and how it is supervised and measured (success rate, cost, time saved). Avoid jargon, give a concrete end-to-end example and talk about risks and costs, not only promises.
key_points: Assistant analogy with a goal, tools and rules
What it does alone vs what requires human approval
It can be wrong: guardrails, supervision, success metrics
Concrete end-to-end example, costs and limits
common_mistakes: Overselling autonomy
Staying in jargon (tokens, prompts, loops)

question: How do you detect and stop infinite planning loops?
reference: Prevention: hard limits on iterations, tokens, time and cost per task; detection: spot repeated identical tool calls (same tool + same arguments), lack of progress (unchanged state, same error), context growing without new results; reaction: interrupt, summarize the state, ask the human for clarification or degrade to a partial answer. Help the model make progress: informative tool results, budget announced in the prompt, ask for an explicit plan and a completion criterion. Trace loops in production to adjust.
key_points: Hard limits: iterations, tokens, time, cost
Detection of repetition (same calls) and lack of progress
Reaction: clean stop, human escalation, partial answer
Explicit tool results and budget to help the model
Traces to analyze loops
common_mistakes: Relying only on the model to stop
Forgetting the cost ceiling

question: How do you implement termination conditions in long-running agents?
reference: Combine several conditions: verified success (passing tests, satisfied rubric, validation by a judge or a human); stop declared by the model (it states the task is done, in an explicit format); resource limits (iterations, tokens, duration, dollar budget); lack of progress or repeated errors; external signals (cancellation, deadline). Make termination observable (stop reason logged) and resumable (state checkpoints) so a run can restart without redoing everything. Define the success condition before launching the agent.
key_points: Objectively verified success (tests, rubric, validation)
Stop declared by the model in an explicit format
Resource ceilings and detection of no progress
Logged stop reason, checkpoints for resuming
Success criterion defined before launch
common_mistakes: A single stop condition (for example only the iteration count)
No verification of a result declared 'done'

question: How do you sandbox tool execution safely?
reference: Run code or commands in an isolated environment (ephemeral container or microVM) with an unprivileged user, file system limited to the project, network cut or allow-listed, CPU, memory, time and output-size limits; no secrets in the sandbox (injected at the egress point or through a proxy); per-tool permissions (read-only by default, destructive actions subject to approval); logging of every action; cleanup of the environment after the task; and argument checks before execution (paths, commands). Treat tool output as untrusted.
key_points: Isolation: ephemeral container/microVM, unprivileged user, restricted FS
Network cut or allow-listed; CPU/memory/time limits
No secrets in the sandbox; per-tool permissions, approval of sensitive actions
Argument validation, logging, cleanup
common_mistakes: Running the code inside the server process
Leaving API keys reachable from the sandbox

question: How do you handle tool failures, retries, and idempotency?
reference: Classify errors: transient (timeout, 429, 5xx) to retry with exponential backoff and jitter, a limited number of times; permanent (400, invalid argument) to return to the model with a clear message so it can correct. Make actions idempotent: idempotency keys on writes, check the state before acting, prefer 'upsert' operations. Save state between steps to resume after a crash. Plan per-tool timeouts, a circuit breaker when a service fails repeatedly, and degradation (partial answer, human escalation). Trace everything for diagnosis.
key_points: Distinguish transient errors (retry with backoff) from permanent ones (back to the model)
Idempotency: idempotency keys, state check, upsert
Timeouts, circuit breaker, maximum number of retries
State checkpoints to resume; graceful degradation
Traceability of failures
common_mistakes: Blindly retrying actions with side effects (double payment, double email)
Hiding the error from the model instead of returning an actionable message

question: What are the biggest security risks with tool-using agents?
reference: Indirect prompt injection: content read by the agent (web page, email, document, tool result) contains instructions that hijack it; data exfiltration through a tool (sending secrets to a URL); destructive or irreversible actions (deletion, payment, sending) triggered by mistake; privilege escalation when the agent has too many rights; uncontrolled code execution; PII leaking into logs. Mitigations: least privilege, separation between untrusted data and instructions, human approval of sensitive actions, sandbox, destination allow-lists, logs and rate limits, adversarial testing.
key_points: Indirect prompt injection through processed content
Data exfiltration and irreversible actions
Excessive rights / privilege escalation, code execution
Mitigations: least privilege, human approval, sandbox, allow-lists, adversarial tests
common_mistakes: Mentioning only the user's direct jailbreak
Believing the system prompt is enough as protection

question: How do you create an agent for analyzing customer support tickets, drafting responses, and escalating complex issues.
reference: Pipeline: ticket classification (category, urgency, sentiment) with structured output; context retrieval (customer history, knowledge base through RAG, order status through tools); drafting a reply grounded on the sources, in the brand's tone; confidence score and escalation rules (sensitive topics, refund above a threshold, low confidence, unhappy customer) to a human with a summary and suggested actions. Human in the loop at first (draft approved), progressive autonomy driven by metrics. Evaluation: annotated ticket set, correct escalation rate, satisfaction, resolution time; guardrails on PII and binding promises.
key_points: Structured classification + context retrieval (RAG, business tools)
Draft grounded on sources, controlled tone
Explicit escalation rules (confidence, sensitive topics, amounts) with a summary for the human
Human in the loop then progressive autonomy
Evaluation on annotated tickets, business metrics, PII guardrails
common_mistakes: Letting the agent answer directly from day one
No measurable escalation criterion

question: Build an agent reviewing code and suggesting improvements.
reference: Inputs: the diff, the affected files with context, the project conventions. Tools: file reading, repository search, running tests and linters in a sandbox. Process: understand the intent of the change, go through the review points (bugs, security, readability, tests, performance), verify each suspicion by reading the code or running it, then produce structured comments (file, line, severity, justification, concrete suggestion), prioritizing real problems over style. Guardrails: do not modify the code without approval, limit noise (confidence threshold), respect the repository rules. Evaluation: precision of findings on annotated PRs, acceptance rate by developers.
key_points: Context: diff + files + conventions; tools for reading, searching, testing
Verify hypotheses before commenting (read, run)
Structured, prioritized comments with a concrete suggestion
Limit noise (confidence), do not modify without approval
Evaluation: precision of findings, acceptance by developers
common_mistakes: Commenting only on style
Producing unverified remarks (false positives) that wear reviewers out

question: How do you ensure the output from LLMs is consistent and accurate?
reference: You do not 'guarantee', you reduce and measure. Design side: structured outputs (JSON schema, validation), low temperature for factual tasks, grounding on sources (RAG) with citations, precise instructions with examples, splitting complex tasks into verifiable steps. Verification side: deterministic validators (schema, business rules, tests for code), LLM judge or verification model for grounding, double pass or voting for critical cases, human in the loop for sensitive ones. Measurement side: reference evaluation set, run on every prompt or model change, production monitoring (error rate, user feedback). Consistency also means pinning model and prompt versions.
key_points: Constrain: validated structured outputs, low temperature, precise instructions and examples
Ground on sources and require citations
Verify: deterministic validators, LLM judge, human for the critical
Measure: evaluation set replayed on every change, production monitoring
Pin model and prompt versions
common_mistakes: Promising guaranteed accuracy
Relying on the prompt alone without verification or evaluation

question: How do you evaluate a chatbot?
reference: Define what 'good' means for the use case: accuracy and grounding of answers, compliance with instructions and tone, safety (appropriate refusals), usefulness (need resolved), concision. Offline: reference conversation set (anonymized real + synthetic, including hard and adversarial cases), rubric scoring by an LLM judge calibrated on human annotations, automatic metrics where they exist (accuracy on known-answer questions), non-regression tests on every change. Online: resolution rate, escalation to a human, satisfaction (CSAT, thumbs), abandonment, latency and cost; A/B tests between versions. Evaluate at the turn level and over the whole conversation (multi-turn).
key_points: Criteria defined by the use case (accuracy, grounding, instructions, safety, usefulness)
Offline evaluation set including hard and adversarial cases
LLM judge with a rubric, calibrated on human annotations; non-regression
Online metrics: resolution, escalation, satisfaction, A/B
Multi-turn evaluation, not only per isolated answer
common_mistakes: Limiting yourself to BLEU/ROUGE or a manual impression
Forgetting evaluation in production

question: What metrics do you consider when evaluating LLM performance?
reference: Task quality: accuracy / success rate on a reference set, F1 or exact match for extraction, pass@k for code, rubric score by a judge for free text, grounding and correct-citation rates in RAG, hallucination rate. Behavior: format compliance (valid JSON), instruction following, appropriate vs excessive refusal rates, bias and safety. Operational: latency (p50/p95, time to first token), cost per request, throughput, API error rate. The choice depends on the use case; generic metrics (perplexity, public benchmarks) matter little next to your own evaluation set.
key_points: Task metrics that fit: accuracy, F1/EM, pass@k, judge rubric
Grounding, hallucinations, citations (RAG)
Compliance: format, instructions, refusals, safety
Operational: latency, cost, throughput, errors
Your own evaluation set over public benchmarks
common_mistakes: Citing only generic benchmarks (MMLU) or perplexity
Forgetting cost and latency

question: How do you build a golden dataset for evaluation?
reference: Start from real usage: sample production queries (anonymized), stratified by type, difficulty and frequency; complement with synthetic cases to cover rare, edge and adversarial cases (unanswerable questions, injections). Annotate with humans: expected answer or criteria rubric, with an annotation guide and double annotation to measure agreement. Aim for a few hundred examples at first, version the set, keep a development set separate from a held-out test set, and enrich it with failures met in production. Check for drift regularly (the product evolves).
key_points: Representative, stratified sampling of real queries
Synthetic cases for rare, edge and adversarial situations
Human annotation with a guide and inter-annotator agreement
Versioning, dev/test split, continuous enrichment with failures
Size: hundreds of examples to start, quality over quantity
common_mistakes: Generating the whole set with an LLM without human validation
Tuning prompts on the test set

question: How do you detect and mitigate hallucinations?
reference: Detection: compare the answer with the sources (grounding by LLM judge or NLI, claim by claim), check citations, measure consistency across several samples (an unstable answer is suspect), use external validators (fact base, code execution, API). Reduction: RAG with the instruction to stick to the context and admit ignorance, low temperature, structured outputs, decomposition into verifiable steps, more capable models, post-processing that removes unsupported claims, human in the loop for the critical. Measure the hallucination rate on an evaluation set with trick questions and track it in production.
key_points: Detection: claim-by-claim grounding check, citations, cross-sample consistency, external validators
Reduction: RAG + abstention instruction, low temperature, decomposition
Post-processing: remove or flag unsupported claims
Continuous measurement with trick questions and production tracking
common_mistakes: Thinking a good prompt eliminates hallucinations
Confusing fluency with accuracy

question: How would you prevent factual errors in a summarization system?
reference: Constrain the model to stay extractive or to cite the source passages for each claim; limit the context length (split long documents, summarize parts then merge); verify faithfulness downstream: each sentence of the summary is checked against the source text by an LLM judge or an NLI model, unsupported sentences are removed or flagged; detect the entities and numbers in the summary and check that they appear in the source; low temperature; evaluate on a set annotated for faithfulness (not only ROUGE) and have a human proofread sensitive documents.
key_points: Grounded summary: extractive or with a citation per claim
Sentence-by-sentence faithfulness check (judge, NLI) and entity/number control
Long documents handled in parts
Faithfulness evaluation beyond ROUGE; human review for the sensitive
common_mistakes: Evaluating only with ROUGE/BLEU
Letting the model 'complete' with its own knowledge

question: How do you debug a RAG chatbot giving confident but wrong answers?
reference: Reproduce with the traces: for each case, look at the query, the retrieved chunks and their scores, the final prompt and the answer. Locate the stage: the right information is not in the index (ingestion); it is in the index but not retrieved (retrieval: embeddings, rewriting, k, filters); it is retrieved but the model ignores it or extrapolates (generation: prompt, context too long, contradictory passages, obsolete documents). Fix the faulty stage, add the case to the evaluation set, and strengthen the guardrails: abstention under a threshold, verified citations, sources displayed so the user can check.
key_points: Start from the traces: query, chunks + scores, final prompt
Locate the stage: ingestion vs retrieval vs generation
Typical causes: information missing, poorly ranked, ignored, contradictory or obsolete documents
Fix then add the case to the evaluation set
Guardrails: abstention, verified citations, visible sources
common_mistakes: Changing the prompt at random without locating the failure
Not checking whether the right information is in the index

question: How do you evaluate a RAG pipeline?
reference: Separate the two stages. Retrieval: question set with annotated relevant passages, measure recall@k, precision@k, MRR/NDCG; compare chunking, embeddings, hybrid, reranking. Generation (with retrieval fixed): faithfulness to the context (grounding), answer relevance, accuracy against a reference answer, correct abstention rate on unanswerable questions, citation quality; scoring by an LLM judge calibrated on human annotations. End to end: rate of correct answers, latency and cost per query. Replay on every change; track user feedback and no-result cases in production.
key_points: Retrieval: recall@k, precision@k, MRR/NDCG on annotated passages
Generation: faithfulness/grounding, relevance, accuracy, correct abstention, citations
LLM judge calibrated on human annotations
End to end: accuracy, latency, cost; non-regression
Production monitoring
common_mistakes: Evaluating only the final answer without isolating retrieval
Forgetting questions whose answer is not in the corpus

question: How do you evaluate agent performance? What metrics matter (tool selection quality, action advancement, context adherence)?
reference: Outcome: task success rate verified objectively (tests, expected final state, rubric) on a varied task set, with several attempts to measure variance. Process: tool-selection quality (right tool, right arguments), action advancement (does each step bring the goal closer?), adherence to context and instructions, absence of loops, recovered errors. Safety: forbidden actions attempted, permission compliance. Efficiency: number of steps, tokens, cost and time per successful task. Evaluate with full traces, per-step judges and reproducible test environments (sandbox, frozen data).
key_points: Objectively verified success rate, over several attempts (variance)
Step quality: tool selection, advancement, context adherence
Safety: forbidden actions, permissions
Efficiency: steps, tokens, cost, time per success
Reproducible test environments and full traces
common_mistakes: Looking only at the final answer
One attempt per task although agents are non-deterministic

question: What operational/business metrics matter for AI systems?
reference: Operational: latency (p50/p95, time to first token), availability and API error rate, throughput, cost per request and per user, token consumption, cache hit rate, timeout and retry rates. Continuous quality: judge scores on a sample, hallucination or ungrounded-answer rate, refusal rate, user feedback (thumbs, reports), input drift. Business: resolution or conversion rate, time saved, escalation rate to a human, satisfaction (CSAT/NPS), retention, cost per outcome. The key is to link technical metrics to business goals and to define alerts.
key_points: Operational: latency, errors, cost, tokens, cache
Continuous quality: judge on a sample, grounding, refusals, user feedback
Business: resolution/conversion, escalation, satisfaction, cost per outcome
Link technical metrics to business goals; alerts
common_mistakes: Tracking only latency and errors
No quality metric after deployment

question: How would you evaluate and monitor a model in production, not just offline?
reference: Log requests, answers, contexts and metadata (with PII handling); sample conversations and score them automatically (LLM judge with a rubric) and by humans on a fraction; collect explicit feedback (thumbs, corrections) and implicit feedback (rephrasing, abandonment, escalation); track input drift (new topics, languages) and output drift (length, refusals); dashboards and threshold alerts; canary and A/B tests for every model or prompt change; close the loop: failures spotted in production feed the offline evaluation set.
key_points: Full traces with PII handling
Automatic scoring of a sample (judge) + partial human review
Explicit and implicit user feedback
Input/output drift, dashboards, alerts
Canary / A/B and loop back to the offline evaluation set
common_mistakes: Assuming offline performance holds
Collecting no user feedback

question: How would you test a new model before full deployment?
reference: Offline: replay the full evaluation set (quality, format, safety, cost, latency) and compare with the current model's results, manually reviewing the differences; check API changes (parameters, behaviors). Shadow mode: run the new model in parallel on real traffic without showing its answers, compare. Canary: expose a small percentage of users with close monitoring and automatic rollback on thresholds. A/B: measure business metrics with statistical significance. Deploy progressively, by segment, keeping the ability to roll back.
key_points: Comparative offline evaluation with review of the differences
Shadow mode on real traffic
Canary with monitoring and automatic rollback
A/B on business metrics
Progressive, reversible deployment
common_mistakes: Switching all traffic after a single manual test
Ignoring format or tone changes that break downstream consumers

question: How do you measure hallucination rate in production?
reference: There is no live ground truth, so you estimate: sample answers regularly, automatically check grounding against the provided sources (LLM judge or NLI, claim by claim) and calibrate that judge on a human-annotated sample to know its precision; complement with user signals (reports, corrections, thumbs down) and cross-sample consistency; track the share of unsupported claims by segment and over time, with alerts; run periodic human audits to recalibrate. For answers without sources (model knowledge), check against fact bases when possible.
key_points: Sampling + automatic claim-by-claim grounding check
Judge calibration on human annotations
User signals and cross-sample consistency
Tracking by segment over time, alerts, periodic human audits
common_mistakes: Assuming it can be measured exactly without annotation
Trusting the judge without calibrating it

question: How do you monitor and observe autonomous agent behavior in production?
reference: Trace each session as a tree: every turn, tool call (arguments, result, duration, error), decision, cost and tokens, with identifiers to link to the user and the task (OpenTelemetry or a dedicated tool). Metrics: success rate, number of steps, loops detected, tool errors, sensitive actions, latency and cost per task. Alerts on drifts (cost explosion, repeated failures, forbidden actions). Replay of problematic sessions for diagnosis, sampling for human review, and a dashboard per agent version to compare after every change.
key_points: Structured traces per session: turns, tools, arguments, results, costs
Metrics: success, steps, loops, errors, sensitive actions, cost
Alerts on drifts and forbidden behaviors
Session replay and human review of a sample
Comparison per agent version
common_mistakes: Logging only the final answer
No limit or alert on cost

question: How do you reduce latency in GenAI applications?
reference: Stream the answer to reduce perceived latency; pick a smaller or faster model when quality allows; shorten prompts and cap output length; prompt caching for stable prefixes; semantic cache for recurring queries; parallelize independent calls (retrieval, sub-tasks); reduce the number of steps in a chain; precompute what can be (embeddings, summaries); optimize retrieval (ANN index, reasonable k); measure where the time goes (time to first token vs generation vs tools) before optimizing.
key_points: Streaming for perceived latency
Faster model, shorter prompts and outputs
Caching (prefix and semantic)
Parallelization, fewer steps, precomputation
Profile first: TTFT vs generation vs tools
common_mistakes: Optimizing without measuring where the time goes
Forgetting that output length often dominates latency

question: What is time to first token and why does it matter for user experience?
reference: TTFT is the delay between sending the request and receiving the first token of the answer; it covers the network, queueing, and prompt processing (prefill, proportional to input size). It determines when the user sees that 'something is happening': with streaming, a short TTFT makes the wait acceptable even if the full answer takes several seconds. Distinct from generation throughput (tokens per second) and from total latency. It is reduced by shortening the prompt, with prompt caching, by avoiding blocking steps before the call and by choosing a faster model.
key_points: Definition: delay until the first token (network + queue + prompt prefill)
Role in perception: with streaming, the wait becomes acceptable
Different from generation throughput and total latency
Levers: shorter prompt, caching, fast model, upstream steps
common_mistakes: Confusing TTFT with total latency
Ignoring that prefill depends on prompt size

question: How would you benchmark each LLM call in a multi-step pipeline to identify latency bottlenecks?
reference: Instrument each step with spans (OpenTelemetry or an LLM tracing tool): step name, model, input and output tokens, TTFT, total duration, tool and retrieval time, errors and retries, cost. Aggregate per step on real traffic: p50/p95, share of total time, variance. Visualize the trace as a waterfall to see what is sequential and could be parallel. Replay a fixed sample of requests as a benchmark to compare variants (shorter prompt, other model, cache). Set latency budgets per step and alerts.
key_points: Spans per step with tokens, TTFT, duration, tools, errors, cost
p50/p95 aggregation and share of total time per step
Waterfall view to spot parallelisable sequential work
Reproducible benchmark on a fixed sample to compare variants
Latency budgets and alerts
common_mistakes: Measuring only end-to-end latency
Comparing variants on different requests

question: How do you reduce token costs?
reference: Reduce input: concise prompts, removal of useless context, more relevant chunks (better retrieval, smaller k), summary or compaction of the history, compact formats for data. Reduce output: ask for short or structured answers, cap max_tokens, avoid verbose reasoning when it adds nothing. Caching: prompt caching on stable prefixes, semantic cache of answers. Routing: small model for simple tasks, large model for the rest; effort level adapted. Batch processing (cheaper batch API) for non-interactive work. Measure cost per request and per feature before and after.
key_points: Input: concise prompts, relevant context, compacted history
Output: short/structured answers, max_tokens
Prefix caching and semantic cache
Routing to cheaper models and adapted effort; batch for asynchronous work
Measure cost per request before/after
common_mistakes: Thinking only about the model's price
Forgetting that output costs more than input

question: Cost vs. quality trade-offs: when is a small open-source model "good enough"?
reference: When the task is well delimited (classification, extraction, rephrasing, routing), when you have an evaluation set to measure the quality gap with a large model, and that gap is acceptable for the business cost of an error; when volume is high and latency or cost are binding; when data must stay on premises (confidentiality); possibly after fine-tuning on the task. It is not good enough for open-ended tasks, long reasoning, complex agentic work, or when you cannot operate the inference (GPU, updates, security). Decide with numbers: measured quality, total cost of ownership, latency.
key_points: Delimited task and evaluation set to measure the gap
Acceptable business error cost; high volume or latency/cost constraints
Confidentiality / on-premise; fine-tuning possible
Unsuitable for open-ended tasks, long reasoning, complex agentic work
Total cost of ownership of inference
common_mistakes: Deciding without measuring quality on your own task
Forgetting the operating cost of a self-hosted model

question: What is model tiering? When do you route to a small distilled model vs. a large LLM?
reference: Tiering means having several models of different size and cost and routing each request to the cheapest one that reaches the required quality. The router can be a rule (task type, length, user), a difficulty classifier, or a cascade: try the small model and escalate to the large one when confidence is low or a validation fails. Small model: simple and frequent tasks, tight latency constraints, pre-filtering; large model: reasoning, open-ended tasks, critical cases, low confidence. Measure quality per tier on an evaluation set and monitor the escalation rate and the real cost (a badly tuned cascade costs more).
key_points: Definition: several models, routing to the cheapest sufficient one
Router: rules, difficulty classifier, cascade with escalation on low confidence
Small model: simple, frequent, latency; large: reasoning, open-ended, critical
Measure quality per tier, escalation rate, real cost
common_mistakes: Routing without measuring the small model's quality
Ignoring the cost of escalations

question: Your app gets 1M queries/day - how do you optimize cost?
reference: Put numbers on it first: cost per request (input/output tokens x price) x volume, per feature. Then act in order of return: caching (prefix and semantic, a share of requests is repetitive), shorter prompts and outputs, routing simple requests to cheaper models, batch API for everything non-interactive, rate limits and per-user quotas against abuse, precomputed embeddings and summaries, and possibly fine-tuning a small model for very high-volume tasks. Measure the impact of each lever on a sample before generalizing, and track cost per request continuously.
key_points: Quantify cost per request and per feature
Caching (prefix, semantic) first
Shorter prompts/outputs, multi-model routing
Batch for asynchronous work, anti-abuse quotas, precomputation
Fine-tuned small model for volume; measure each lever
common_mistakes: Switching models without quantifying
Forgetting the repetitiveness of requests (cache)

question: Estimate the budget for a RAG pipeline at enterprise scale (e.g., 300,000 legal contracts).
reference: Reason by cost item with explicit assumptions. Ingestion (once + updates): 300,000 contracts x ~30 pages x ~500 tokens ~ 4.5 billion tokens to chunk and embed; embedding cost from a few hundred to a few thousand dollars depending on the model, plus extraction/OCR and compute. Storage: ~5 to 10 million chunks x vector dimension -> tens of GB, managed or self-hosted vector database (hundreds to thousands of dollars per month). Queries: requests per day x (question embedding + ~5-10k context tokens + output) x model price; for example 10,000 requests/day at ~$0.02-0.05 ~ $200-500/day. Add evaluation, humans for annotation, infrastructure and a margin. Present a range and the sensitive assumptions (document size, model, volume).
key_points: Break down: ingestion (extraction, embeddings), storage/index, queries, evaluation and humans
Orders of magnitude: tokens per document x number of documents
Query cost = (context + output) x price x volume
Explicit assumptions and a range; sensitivities (size, model, volume)
common_mistakes: Giving a figure without assumptions
Forgetting the recurring cost of queries or of the index infrastructure

question: When and how would you implement LLM guardrails?
reference: As soon as a system is exposed to users or acts on data: guardrails on input (detection of injection, forbidden content, PII, off-topic), on output (format and business-rule validation, toxicity filters, grounding check, PII removal), and on actions (permissions, human approval for the irreversible, rate and cost limits). Layered implementation: fast deterministic rules, classifiers or small models, LLM judge for the nuanced; proportionate to impact (an internal assistant does not have the same requirements as a public chatbot); measure false positives (wrongful refusals) and false negatives with adversarial tests, and log every trigger.
key_points: Three control points: input, output, actions
Layers: deterministic rules, classifiers, LLM judge
Proportionate to risk and exposure
Measure false positives/negatives, adversarial tests, logging
common_mistakes: A single output filter
Ignoring the cost of wrongful refusals on user experience

question: How do you handle data privacy and PII in prompts and logs?
reference: Minimize: send the model only the data it needs; pseudonymize or mask PII before the call (detection by rules and NER, replacement with reversible tokens when the model must reason over them); choose providers with contractual commitments (no training on the data, limited retention, regions) or self-host for the very sensitive; logs: PII masking, encryption, access control, limited retention, separation of technical traces from content; compliance (GDPR: legal basis, right to erasure, DPIA); regular leak tests on outputs and logs.
key_points: Minimization and PII pseudonymization/masking before the call
Provider choice: no training, retention, region; self-hosting when needed
Logs: masking, encryption, restricted access, limited retention
Regulatory compliance (GDPR) and leak tests
common_mistakes: Logging everything in clear text 'for debugging'
Forgetting that model outputs can contain PII

question: How do you protect against prompt injection and jailbreaking?
reference: Assume no prompt-side defense is watertight. Architecture: clearly separate instructions from data (markup, system messages), treat all external content (documents, pages, tool results) as untrusted, limit capabilities (least privilege, no dangerous tools reachable from an untrusted context, human approval for sensitive actions), destination allow-lists. Detection: injection and jailbreak classifiers on input, output monitoring (system prompt leak, forbidden content). Hardening: clear priority instructions, recent better-trained models, continuous adversarial testing (red teaming) and logging of attempts. The goal is to limit impact, not only to block.
key_points: No prompt defense is watertight: limit the impact
Separate instructions from data; external content = untrusted
Least privilege, human approval, allow-lists
Input/output detection and continuous red teaming
common_mistakes: Believing a sentence like 'ignore malicious instructions' is enough
Thinking only of the user as the attacker (forgetting indirect injection)

question: How would you build a system that detects whether content violates policy or contains offensive material?
reference: Define the policy as precise categories with examples and edge cases (harassment, hate, violence, sexual, spam...) and severity levels. Layered pipeline: fast rules (lists, regex) for the obvious, a classifier trained on annotated data (or a moderation API) for volume, an LLM with the policy in the prompt for ambiguous cases, a human for the gray zone and appeals. Data: representative annotated set, with inter-annotator agreement, adversarial samples, balance across languages and dialects. Measure precision/recall per category, pick thresholds according to the cost of false positives and negatives, monitor drift, and offer users a way to appeal.
key_points: Explicit policy: categories, severity, examples and edge cases
Layered pipeline: rules, classifier, LLM, human
Quality annotated set (agreement, adversarial, linguistic diversity)
Precision/recall per category, thresholds by error cost
Drift, appeals, audit
common_mistakes: A single LLM with a vague prompt
Not measuring per category nor handling false positives

question: Your application generates code that gets executed. How do you prevent malicious code generation and execution?
reference: Never run generated code in a trusted environment: isolated, ephemeral sandbox (container/microVM), no network or an allow-list, no secrets, with time, CPU, memory and disk limits and an unprivileged user. Before execution: static analysis (forbidden imports, system calls, network or file access outside the perimeter), library allow-list, human approval for actions with side effects. Input control: the user or a document can inject malicious instructions into the prompt. After: log, cap output size, destroy the environment. Regular adversarial testing.
key_points: Isolated, ephemeral sandbox with no network or secrets and resource limits
Static analysis and allow-lists before execution
Human approval for side effects; least privilege
Injection through the input: untrusted content
Logging, environment destruction, red teaming
common_mistakes: Filtering the code by keywords and running it on the server
Leaving credentials reachable in the execution environment

question: When would you fine-tune vs use prompt engineering vs RAG?
reference: Start with prompt engineering (fast, no annotated data, reversible); move to RAG when the need is to access external, private or changing knowledge, with traceability; use fine-tuning when the model's behavior must change rather than its knowledge: very specific style or format, narrow high-volume task where a small fine-tuned model beats a large model on cost/latency, prompt-length reduction, domain with particular vocabulary. Fine-tuning requires quality data and an evaluation, and is not suited to injecting fresh facts (retraining needed). The approaches combine (RAG + fine-tuned model).
key_points: Order: prompt -> RAG -> fine-tuning, from least to most costly
RAG for external/fresh knowledge with traceability
Fine-tuning for behavior (style, format, narrow task, cost/latency at volume)
Fine-tuning unsuited to changing facts; requires data and evaluation
Combinations possible
common_mistakes: Fine-tuning to 'learn' documents
Skipping prompt engineering

question: What is instruction tuning and how does it differ from pre-training?
reference: Pre-training trains the model to predict the next token on a massive unannotated corpus: it acquires language, knowledge and general abilities, but yields a model that continues text rather than answering. Instruction tuning is supervised fine-tuning on (instruction, desired answer) pairs, far smaller in volume, which teaches the model to follow instructions, adopt a dialogue format and an assistant behavior. It is often followed by preference alignment (RLHF, DPO). It creates no new knowledge: it reveals and steers what pre-training learned.
key_points: Pre-training: next-token prediction, massive unannotated corpus, general abilities
Instruction tuning: supervised fine-tuning on instruction/answer pairs
Goal: follow instructions, assistant format; far smaller volume
Often complemented by RLHF/DPO; adds no knowledge
common_mistakes: Confusing instruction tuning with RLHF
Thinking instruction tuning teaches facts

question: What is PEFT/LoRA and when would you use it?
reference: PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning) covers methods that train only a small fraction of the parameters. LoRA freezes the model weights and adds, on some matrices (attention, MLP), a low-rank correction dW = A.B with small A and B; only A and B are trained (often < 1% of the parameters). Benefits: reduced memory and compute (QLoRA combines it with quantization of the base model), lightweight adapters swappable per task, less catastrophic forgetting. Use it when fine-tuning a large model on a limited GPU, for style/format/domain adaptations, or to maintain several variants. Limits: less adaptation capacity than full fine-tuning for deep changes; hyperparameters (rank, alpha, target modules) to tune.
key_points: PEFT: train only a small fraction of the parameters
LoRA: frozen weights + low-rank correction A.B on some matrices
Benefits: memory/compute, lightweight adapters per task, less forgetting; QLoRA
When: limited resources, style/domain adaptation, multiple variants
Limits: weaker than full fine-tuning for deep changes
common_mistakes: Describing LoRA as a model compression
Forgetting that the base model is still needed at inference

question: Explain the RLHF pipeline: supervised fine-tuning, reward model training, and PPO. How does DPO simplify this?
reference: RLHF: 1) SFT, supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations of good answers; 2) a reward model trained on human comparisons (answer A preferred over B) to predict a score; 3) reinforcement optimization (PPO): the model generates, the reward scores, you maximize the reward with a KL penalty so as not to drift too far from the SFT model and to avoid reward hacking. It is costly and unstable (four models in memory, delicate hyperparameters). DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) removes the reward model and the RL: it derives a classification loss directly on preferred/rejected pairs, with the reference model as an implicit anchor; simpler and more stable, but offline (no exploration) and sensitive to pair quality.
key_points: SFT on demonstrations
Reward model learned from human comparisons
PPO: maximize the reward with a KL penalty; cost and instability
DPO: direct loss on preference pairs, no reward model nor RL
DPO limits: offline, depends on pair quality
common_mistakes: Confusing the reward model with the reference model
Saying DPO needs no preference data

question: Explain quantization. What are the trade-offs between model size, speed, and accuracy?
reference: Quantization represents the weights (and sometimes the activations) with fewer bits: FP16/BF16 -> INT8 -> INT4, or even less. It reduces memory (a 7B model goes from ~14 GB in FP16 to ~4 GB in INT4), speeds up inference when the hardware supports it (less memory bandwidth, integer kernels) and lets you serve larger models on a given GPU. Methods: post-training (PTQ, with calibration: GPTQ, AWQ) or quantization-aware training. Cost: precision loss, small in INT8, more visible in INT4 and on small models or reasoning tasks; some sensitive layers stay in higher precision. Always re-evaluate the quantized model on your own task.
key_points: Principle: fewer bits per weight/activation (FP16 -> INT8 -> INT4)
Gains: memory, bandwidth, speed (with suitable hardware), larger models on one GPU
Methods: PTQ (GPTQ, AWQ, calibration) vs QAT
Precision loss grows with aggressiveness; small models and reasoning more sensitive
Re-evaluate on your task
common_mistakes: Confusing quantization with distillation/pruning
Claiming quantization is always lossless

question: How do you convert implicit user behavior (edits, acceptance, rejection) into training signals for model improvement?
reference: Log events with their context (prompt, answer, action: accepted as is, edited with the final version, rejected, regenerated); derive labels: acceptance = positive example for SFT, edit = pair (initial answer rejected, edited version preferred) for DPO or a reward model, rejection/regeneration = negative or pair with the answer finally kept. Beware of biases: position, inattentive users, edits for reasons unrelated to quality; weight by confidence, filter, deduplicate, aggregate per user. Respect privacy (consent, anonymization). Validate on an annotated set that the implicit signal correlates with quality before training on it, then measure the effect in an A/B test.
key_points: Log events with full context
Mapping: acceptance -> SFT positive; edit -> preference pair; rejection -> negative
Bias and noise: filter, weight, deduplicate
Privacy and consent
Validate the signal/quality correlation then measure in A/B
common_mistakes: Taking every edit as a signal of poor quality
Training on the data without bias handling or validation

question: How would you design a model that can solve math problems? Walk through data collection, supervised fine-tuning, post-training, and evaluation.
reference: Data: problems with step-by-step solutions and verifiable final answers (existing sets, LLM synthesis verified by execution or a solver, diversity of levels and domains), decontamination against the test benchmarks. SFT: start from a strong base model, fine-tune on detailed reasoning (chain-of-thought) with an explicit final-answer format. Post-training: rejection sampling (keep the solutions whose answer is correct), then reinforcement learning with a verifiable reward (exact answer, tests), possibly a process reward model; teach tool use (calculation, code). Evaluation: accuracy on held-out sets (several levels), pass@k and majority vote, error analysis by type, robustness to rephrasing.
key_points: Data: step-by-step solutions, verifiable answers, diversity, decontamination
SFT on detailed reasoning with an explicit final answer
Post-training: rejection sampling, RL with a verifiable reward, tools (code)
Evaluation: held-out sets, pass@k, error analysis, robustness
common_mistakes: Training only on final answers without reasoning
Evaluating on contaminated data

question: How do transformers work?
reference: A Transformer processes a sequence of tokens in parallel. Each token is converted into an embedding to which position information is added (positional encoding or RoPE). Then a stack of identical blocks: a multi-head self-attention layer where each position computes queries, keys and values and weights the other positions by query-key similarity (with a causal mask for generation), followed by a feed-forward network applied position by position, each with a residual connection and normalization. The output is projected onto the vocabulary to predict the next token. Parallelism over the sequence makes training efficient on GPUs; attention cost grows as O(n^2) with length.
key_points: Embeddings + position information
Blocks: multi-head self-attention (Q, K, V, causal mask) + feed-forward
Residual connections and normalization
Final projection onto the vocabulary; next-token prediction
Parallelism in training; O(n^2) attention
common_mistakes: Describing a recurrence (like an RNN)
Forgetting position information

question: What is the self-attention mechanism?
reference: For each token, three vectors are computed by linear projection: query Q, key K, value V. The attention score between a token and every other is the dot product Q.K, divided by the square root of the dimension then passed through a softmax, which gives weights; the output is the weighted sum of the values V. Each token thus builds a contextual representation that depends on the relevant tokens, whatever their distance. Several heads in parallel capture different kinds of relations, then are concatenated and projected. In a decoder, a causal mask prevents looking at the future. Complexity is quadratic in sequence length.
key_points: Q, K, V projections per token
Scores = softmax(QK^T / sqrt(d)), output = weighted sum of the V
Contextual representation independent of distance
Multi-head for several kinds of relations; causal mask in generation
O(n^2) complexity
common_mistakes: Confusing attention with embedding
Forgetting the sqrt(d) scaling and the softmax

question: Explain the difference between encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder Transformer architectures. When would you use each?
reference: Encoder-only (BERT): bidirectional attention, trained by token masking; produces contextual representations: ideal for classification, NER, embeddings, search (bi-encoders, cross-encoders), but does not generate text. Decoder-only (GPT, Llama, Claude): causal attention, trained to predict the next token; text generation, chat, reasoning, in-context learning; this is the architecture of today's LLMs. Encoder-decoder (T5, BART): the encoder reads the input bidirectionally, the decoder generates while attending to the encoder; suited to sequence-to-sequence tasks (translation, summarization) with a clear input/output separation. Today, large-scale decoder-only models cover most generative uses; encoders remain widely used for embeddings and efficient classification.
key_points: Encoder-only: bidirectional, masking, representations -> classification, NER, embeddings
Decoder-only: causal, next token -> generation, chat, today's LLMs
Encoder-decoder: sequence-to-sequence (translation, summarization)
Choice by task: understanding/embeddings vs generation
common_mistakes: Saying BERT generates text
Ignoring the continued use of encoders for embeddings

question: What is KV cache? How does it help in LLM inference?
reference: In autoregressive generation, each new token must attend to all previous tokens. Without a cache, the keys K and values V of the whole sequence would be recomputed at every step for every layer. The KV cache stores those already-computed K and V; at each step only the Q, K, V of the new token are computed and it attends to the cache, which brings the per-token cost from quadratic to linear in length. Cost: GPU memory proportional to layers x heads x length x dimension, which limits batch size and context; hence techniques such as multi-query/grouped-query attention, cache quantization, paged attention. API prompt caching reuses the KV cache of a prefix across requests.
key_points: Problem: recomputing the K/V of the whole sequence for every token
Solution: store K and V per layer, compute only the new token
Gain: linear instead of quadratic per-token cost
Memory cost -> GQA/MQA, quantization, paged attention
Link with prompt caching
common_mistakes: Confusing the KV cache with a response cache
Forgetting the memory cost

question: What is Mixture of Experts (MoE)? How does it improve efficiency?
reference: In an MoE, the feed-forward layer of each block is replaced by several 'expert' sub-networks and a router that, for each token, selects a small number of experts (top-k, often 1 or 2). The model therefore has many parameters in total (capacity) but activates only a fraction per token (compute). At comparable quality, this reduces training and inference cost per token compared with a dense model of the same capacity. Trade-offs: all expert memory must be loaded (memory and communication cost), load balancing across experts (auxiliary losses), trickier training, more sensitive fine-tuning.
key_points: Several FFN experts + top-k router per token
High total parameters, few active parameters -> reduced compute per token
Gain in training/inference cost at a given capacity
Trade-offs: total memory, expert balancing, training complexity
common_mistakes: Believing MoE reduces the required memory
Describing an ensemble of complete models

question: What are the differences between BPE, WordPiece, and character-level tokenization? What are the trade-offs?
reference: Tokenization splits text into units. Character level: tiny vocabulary, no unknown word, but very long sequences (attention cost) and units carrying little meaning. BPE (GPT, Llama): starts from characters/bytes and iteratively merges the most frequent pairs up to the desired vocabulary size; frequent subwords become one token, rare words are split; the byte-level variant handles any text without an unknown token. WordPiece (BERT): similar but picks the merges that maximize the corpus likelihood, with the '##' prefix for continuations. Trade-offs: vocabulary size vs sequence length, coverage of languages and code (an English-biased vocabulary costs other languages more tokens), handling of numbers and case. The tokeniser is frozen with the model.
key_points: Character: no unknowns, long sequences, little semantics
BPE: frequency-based merges, subwords; byte-level without unknown tokens
WordPiece: likelihood-based merges, ## prefix (BERT)
Trade-offs: vocabulary vs length, multilingual/code coverage, numbers
Tokeniser tied to the model
common_mistakes: Saying LLMs tokenize by words
Ignoring the effect of tokenization on cost by language
